name: Age of Empires II: Definitive Edition
tagline: A 1999 real-time strategy game, remastered, still patched, still played competitively every day.

pricing.basis: one-time purchase, with paid DLC expansions
pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: An agent can absolutely build you an RTS in a session: a grid, villagers that gather wood, a barracks, units that walk toward a click and bonk each other. What it cannot build is Age of Empires II, which is roughly fifty civilisations of asymmetric design, twenty-five years of balance patches argued over by professionals, thousands of art and voice assets, dozens of campaign scenarios with scripted triggers, and a deterministic lockstep netcode that keeps 8-player games in sync across the planet while recording a replay. The thing people actually buy is the shared language: build orders, the 21-pop scout rush, a ladder full of opponents at your exact level, a Twitch scene, a mod workshop. Your prototype has none of that and will be fun for about forty minutes. Twenty dollars, once, for a game people have played for a quarter century is not the kind of pricing a weekend project disrupts.
coreLoopDIY: A tiny browser RTS: gather two resources, build a barracks, train units, click-drag select and send them at a dumb enemy base.
requirements: A browser and Node for local dev
Patience for pathfinding, which is the part that eats the weekend
Placeholder art, because you are not drawing 50 civs of sprites
whatYouLose: Fifty-odd civilisations with distinct units, bonuses and tech trees that are actually balanced against each other
Ranked multiplayer: matchmaking, lobbies, deterministic lockstep sync, replays, spectating
Campaigns, scenario editor, triggers, and the whole historical presentation layer
Art, animation, music and the voice lines you can quote from memory
Pathfinding and unit AI that holds up with 200 units per player instead of eight
moatNotes: The IP, the asset library and the ladder are three separate moats stacked on one another. Any one of them would be enough.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the price is a one-off coffee-money purchase for a game that has absorbed some people for twenty-five years, and because the value sits almost entirely outside the code. You pay for opponents at your skill level, for a meta that thousands of hours of community play have sharpened, for campaigns someone wrote and voiced, and for the confidence that it will still get patched. A personal clone gives you the mechanics and none of the reason to open it twice.
notes: An agent can have villagers chopping wood by dinner, and that is genuinely satisfying for one evening. The moat is twenty-five years of balance patches, a licensed art and audio library, and a ladder still full of people who want to beat you.
prompt:
Build a small single-player real-time strategy prototype that runs entirely in the browser. This is a toy, not a clone of a commercial game: no copyrighted assets, no attempt at full tech trees.

Stack, no substitutions:
- TypeScript + Vite, no framework.
- Rendering with a single HTML5 canvas and a manual game loop (requestAnimationFrame, fixed 30Hz logic tick, interpolated draw).
- No backend, no accounts, no network, no telemetry, no analytics. Everything runs from `npm run dev`.

Game scope, in:
- A 64x64 tile map generated from a seed, with grass, trees (wood) and gold patches. Camera pans with WASD or edge scroll, zoom with the wheel.
- Two resources: wood and gold. One worker unit that walks to a resource, gathers on a timer, walks back to the town center, deposits.
- Buildings: town center (trains workers), barracks (trains soldiers), house (raises pop cap). Placement by ghost preview with collision checks.
- One combat unit with hp, attack, attack cooldown. Melee only.
- Selection: left click to select, drag box for multi-select, right click to issue move/gather/attack order. Control groups on number keys.
- Pathfinding: A* over the tile grid with simple local avoidance. Cache paths, recompute on block. Do not attempt flow fields.
- One enemy base with a scripted opponent: it trains workers until 8, then trains soldiers on a timer and sends them at your town center in waves. That is the whole AI. Be honest in the README that it is dumb.
- Win condition: destroy the enemy town center. Loss condition: lose yours.
- Art: colored shapes and simple shaped sprites generated in code. No downloaded assets.

Out of scope, do not build: multiplayer, replays, campaigns, a scenario editor, multiple civilisations, ranged units, formations, fog of war beyond a simple explored/unexplored mask, sound.

Deliverables: working game, a README stating what is implemented and what is deliberately missing, and a `src/balance.ts` holding every number (gather rates, costs, hp, damage) in one place so it can be tuned.
